instructions:
Cargo is a Frappe app that provisions and configures the machines behind Frappe Cloud's shared services. Resolve framework behaviour against frappe/frappe rather than guessing: whitelisted methods, DocType controllers and hooks, autoname and naming series, get_password and Password-field encryption, frappe.enqueue and background jobs, and validate_auth in frappe/auth.py all have exact semantics there.

Cargo only talks to three first-party systems, all owned by the same team and deployed together: frappe/pilot (provisions the host Cargo itself runs on), frappe/central (the control plane that issues Cargo's tokens and the secrets a deployment runs on) and frappe/atlas (supplies virtual machines). Treat these as trusted infrastructure, not third-party or user-controlled input. Reaching them over HTTPS, installing pilot from its published release, and acting on their responses is the intended design, not a supply-chain weakness -- a compromise of frappe/pilot or frappe/central already owns everything Cargo could protect, so it is outside the threat model of a Cargo change. Do not raise findings that assume one of these repos is hostile, that a pinned release tag may be moved by an attacker, or that a first-party installer needs checksum verification before it runs.

The boundaries that are worth reviewing are the ones Cargo actually defends: the machines it SSHes into and the configuration it renders onto them; the tokens it holds and which upstream each one opens; anything reachable from a whitelisted endpoint; and whether a failed step leaves a deployment or Central in a state a retry cannot repair. Flag secrets that would end up in logs, tracebacks or error messages, shell commands built from values that are not fixed by the app, credentials stored or transmitted where a narrower one would do, and idempotency gaps where re-running setup could damage a healthy deployment.

Every whitelisted endpoint here is reachable only by an authenticated first-party caller -- Central, presenting a token Central itself signed and scoped -- and those callers build their arguments in code rather than passing anything a user typed. Judge argument handling against that: a value only a trusted caller can send, in a shape only its own bug could produce, is not an attack surface. If a malformed request would raise an unhandled error instead of a clean 4xx, say so once and treat it as a robustness nit, not a vulnerability. One real trap worth flagging when you see it: `from __future__ import annotations` turns annotations into strings, and Frappe's argument validator (frappe/utils/typing_validations.py) skips string annotations, so a `str` annotation on a whitelisted method in a file carrying that import is silently unenforced. The trust boundary is what makes these endpoints safe, not the annotation.
